hints: Look at the overall shape of the graph and notice where the big drops occur, as these tell you when a new period starts.
Identify P and Q first. P is a very high peak followed by a sharp fall to Q, so think about which type of elements these must be.
Focus on the two small dips within the Q to X section, from R to S and from U to V, and recall why Group 13 and Group 16 are lower than expected.
walkthrough:
**Spot the noble gases and the new period**

Think of first ionisation energy as how tightly the outer electron is held. Noble gases hold it tightest, so they are the tall peaks.

Here P is a tall peak, then the value crashes down to Q. That crash means a new shell has started, so Q is an alkali metal in the next period.

**Label the Q to X period**

From Q the trend generally rises to the next tall peak X. This is one full period, like Na to Ar in Period 3.

Within it, Q is Group 1, R is Group 2, S is Group 13, T is Group 14, U is Group 15, V is Group 16, W is Group 17, X is Group 18.

**Explain the two small dips**

The dip from R ($ns^2$) to S ($ns^2 np^1$) happens because the new $p$ electron is higher in energy, more shielded and easier to remove.

$$\text{R } (ns^2) \rightarrow \text{S } (ns^2 np^1): \text{ p electron is more shielded}$$

**Explain the U to V dip**

U has configuration $ns^2 np^3$ with three unpaired $p$ electrons. V has $ns^2 np^4$ where two electrons must share one $p$ orbital.

$$\text{U } (np_x^1 np_y^1 np_z^1) \rightarrow \text{V } (np_x^2 np_y^1 np_z^1)$$ 
That paired electron in V repels its partner, making it easier to remove, so ionisation energy drops slightly.

options.A: Incorrect. P and X are both noble gas peaks, but P is the end of one period and X is the end of the next period. The sharp fall from P to Q shows Q starts a new period, so P and X are in different periods.
options.B: Incorrect. Across a period from Q to X, proton number increases and electrons are added to the same shell. Nuclear charge increases and atomic radius decreases, so the outer electron is held more strongly. It is increasing nuclear charge, not increasing radius, that causes the general rise.
options.C: Incorrect. R is Group 2 ($3s^2$) and S is Group 13 ($3s^2 3p^1$). The fall is because the $3p$ electron is in a higher energy subshell, further out and with extra shielding by the $3s$ electrons, so it is easier to remove. Shielding has increased, not decreased.
options.D: Correct. U is Group 15 with three unpaired p electrons and V is Group 16 with one paired p electrons. The spin-pair repulsion in the doubly occupied orbital in V makes that electron easier to remove, giving the small dip from U to V.
